title: Walking God home
hook: the sky is dark with clouds, and Radha is told to take him home
carry: bhakti: the lord of all, close enough to love
tomorrow: Radha at the edge of the dance

segments.voice: Yesterday, puja: Sudama's handful of rice, and Krishna's word that offered with love, a leaf is enough for God.
screen: `SUDAMA'S HANDFUL OF RICE.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.`

segments.voice: The sky is heavy with clouds. The forest is dark with tamala trees. Night is coming on, and the boy is nervous. So Nanda, the cowherd chief, turns to Radha: take him home. That's how the Gita Govinda begins, with a walk home through the dark. And the verse hails what follows on the bank of the river Yamuna: the secret love of Radha and Madhava, one of Krishna's names. After our days on the Bhagavad Gita, the path turns from Krishna the teacher on a battlefield to Krishna the beloved in a forest.
screen: `CLOUDS, DARK TREES, NIGHT.` → `TAKE HIM HOME.` → `FROM BATTLEFIELD TO FOREST.`

segments.voice: Gita Govinda means the song of Govinda, the cowherd, another name for Krishna. It's a love poem, and it says so up front. A few lines in, Jayadeva gives an invitation. If your heart is moved by remembering Hari, and if you're curious about the arts of love, then listen to these sweet, soft, lovely words. Remembering God and the play of lovers, offered as one door. Then, before the love story starts, Jayadeva sings a hymn through the Lord's descents into the world, the avatars: the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf, and on through Rama and the Buddha to Kalki, one stanza each. Every stanza ends with the same refrain: jaya jagadisha hare, victory to you, Hari, Lord of the world. So the reader meets the cosmic Lord first, the one who saves worlds in many forms, and only then the nervous boy Radha is walking home under the clouds. Same Lord. That's one of bhakti's boldest teachings, named plainly: the God of the whole universe comes close enough to be loved like a person, a child to be walked home, a beloved. You don't have to shrink God to love God up close. For centuries the Gita Govinda has been sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri, and Odissi dancers still perform its songs. Jayadeva doesn't explain the paradox. He just sings it.
screen: `THE SONG OF GOVINDA, THE COWHERD.` · `A HYMN TO THE LORD'S DESCENTS.` · `THE COSMIC LORD, THEN THE BOY.` · `CLOSE ENOUGH TO LOVE.` · then, large: `JAYA JAGADISHA HARE.`

segments.voice: Hear the opening again: clouds, dark trees, night coming, and Radha asked to walk the boy home. Now let two pictures sit side by side: the Lord of the whole world, fish, tortoise, man-lion, and the boy under the clouds. If you pray, let the refrain move quietly with the breath, jaya jagadisha hare, the way it's still sung at home and in temples. If not, simply hold the two pictures together, something vast and someone near, and breathe.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda, it's love for the Lord of the world, close enough to walk home.
Your line: bhakti, the Lord of all, close enough to love. Tomorrow, spring, and Radha at the edge of the dance. That's day nine hundred seventy-five.

screen: `DAY 975 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: RADHA AT THE EDGE OF THE DANCE.`

howItsDone: The Gita Govinda has been sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri for centuries; its songs are sung in Hindu devotional settings and performed in classical music and Odissi dance, and the hymn to the avatars with its refrain jaya jagadisha hare is sung on its own as well.

fork.setup: you're the poet. before the love story, you sing the Lord saving the world as a fish, a tortoise, a man-lion. why start there?
options: to show the boy in the forest is the same Lord of the whole world.
because the love story is too small to be about God.
to warn readers away from loving Krishna like a person.
fork.reveal: Jayadeva praises the Lord in every descent, then shows him as the boy Radha walks home: in bhakti, the Lord of all comes close enough to love.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: bhakti, devotion, loving attention.

trapdoor: what you thought: the God who runs the universe is too big to love like a person.
what it means: the Gita Govinda praises Hari in all his descents, then shows him as a nervous boy Radha walks home: bhakti loves the Lord up close.
what a scholar hears: Gita Govinda 1.1–1.3, the dark-clouds opening and Jayadeva's invitation, followed by the hymn to the avatars with its refrain jaya jagadisha hare.
recall: the cowherd women who loved Krishna

chat.says: odissi class is doing a gita govinda piece for the temple recital!! first song is all fish, turtle, boar... sam: 'why does a LOVE poem start with a fish?' 🐟😂
options: the fish and the boy are the same Lord: first Lord of the world, then close enough to love.
the fish is a joke to warm up the crowd before the real story.
it's a different poem stuck on the front. it has nothing to do with Krishna.
chat.meaning: Jayadeva first sings Hari in all his descents, then shows him as a boy Radha walks home. That's bhakti: the Lord of all, close enough to love.

tie.story: Jayadeva sang the Lord saving the world as a fish, a tortoise, a man-lion and more, then showed him as a nervous boy Radha walks home in the dark.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam the fish is the point: the same Lord of the world comes close enough to love.
tie.you: where does God feel too far away to love?

Gita Govinda.meaning: the song of Govinda: Jayadeva's love poem of Radha and Krishna

Jayadeva.meaning: the poet who wrote the Gita Govinda

Nanda.meaning: the cowherd chief who raised Krishna

Yamuna.meaning: the river beside Krishna's cowherd village

Radha.meaning: the cowherd girl Krishna loves in the Gita Govinda

Jagannath.meaning: Lord of the world: Krishna as worshiped at Puri

notes: Editor: hook no longer says the love 'begins' on the walk (the verse hails the secret love-play on the Yamuna bank); 'Devotees hold both at once' (a claim about all devotees) changed to a statement about the poem.
No date is given for Jayadeva or the poem, per the claims rule.

Opening verse (meghair meduram ambaram...) is paraphrased; who speaks the instruction is traditionally read as Nanda; confirm. The verse's sense of the boy being 'timid' (bhirur ayam) rendered as 'nervous'.
Verse numbering: the invitation (yadi hari-smarane sarasam mano...) is given as 1.3; confirm numbering in the edition used.

The avatar list in the teach stops at Rama ('and on through Rama') and does not number the forms, per the claims rule; the hymn later names Balarama, the Buddha and Kalki. A Keeper may choose to list them.
'Read by some devotees as the soul's longing for God': a soft general claim; confirm.
Edwin Arnold's 'The Indian Song of Songs' (1875) is a public-domain version, but no wording was quoted from it.

Audit 2026-10-01: fixed a reversal in the teach ('the young man walking a girl home'): in 1.1 Radha is told to take the timid boy, Krishna, home. The avatar line no longer implies the hymn ends at Rama; it now runs on through the Buddha to Kalki (forms still not counted).
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
